newsitem.title: UK: Brent deal heard at Aug +7 cts, other grades quiet.
newsitem.headline: Brent deal heard at Aug +7 cts, other grades quiet.

text.p: Brent blend crude was reported traded at strong numbers on Monday against the backdrop of a stalemate in business on other North Sea grades, traders said.
The Brent cargo, loading July 17-19, was heard passed from a trader to a Scandinavian buyer at August Brent +7 cents.
The deal, which could not be immediately confirmed, was believed some 10 cents more expensive than the four secretively-priced Brent cargo trades done last Tuesday.
Short-term swaps for this week firmed dramatically on the trade, jumping to around six to seven cents against August, from flat when the day began.

With most of the already nominated July programme in the hands of a European major, wet Brent supply was tight. Demand from an oil company to fill a VLCC committed into the U.S. Gulf was also helping to boost values, traders said.
But differentials on non-Brent cargoes were under pressure, with buyers waiting for sellers to crack, and sellers convinced sufficient demand existed for third decade cargoes to keep numbers high.
"Right now we've got a balance of weak demand against weak supply," said one crude trader. "It will be interesting to see who is the first to price their oil downwards."
But neither buyers nor sellers seemed in a hurry to break the lassitude of a Monday and do business.
Both Brent cargoes turning wet from the paper chains and due to load on July 22-24 were kept by French refiner Elf, traders said.

Cash Brent business was thin, with spreads largely steady. August/September traded twice at -11 cents and once at -12 cents while contracts for differences were also dull, with July 10-11 trading against August early in the day at -2 cents.

In the Mediterranean sentiment diverged over where Russian Urals should be priced, with some saying the few remaining July cargoes were being discussed around Dated Brent -75 cents a barrel on the basis that, with most end-user needs satisfied, demand was thin.

But others said that since Iraqi barrels were still absent, last week's high numbers persisted. They pointed to talk of a deal between a Russian supplier and a Swiss trader at around -70 to -65 cents.
West African markets were thin, with dealers waiting for the release of the Nigerian loading programme for August, expected some time later this week.
